extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and courts considering patent specifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what a patent specification must contain and how it should be drafted: clarity of claim, enablement, disclosure of best mode and modes of application, and limits when claiming improvements versus new machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaim prior matter and state improvement distinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: he should then disclaim the invention of the thing thus referred to or described, and state distinctly his improvement as the thing which he claims to have invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a specification refers to prior devices or matter, the patentee must disclaim the prior invention and clearly identify the improvement claimed as his invention. This prevents claiming old subject-matter as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not monopolize more than invented / avoid dwelling on immaterial or known things
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction will be against the patentee that he seeks to monopolize more than he has invented, or that, by dwelling in his description on things that are immaterial or known, he endeavors to deceive the public, who are not to be deterred from using anything that is old by its appearing in the specification as newly invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the whole subject and point out parts which are old and well known. Over-describing known matter or including immaterial details can be construed as an attempt to extend monopoly and may be fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vagueness/ambiguity in manner of description (distinct from term ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vagueness and ambiguity in the manner of describing the invention which makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ambiguous directions such as 'take any quantity of lead and calcine it, or minium, or red lead' (uncertain whether minium/red lead are to be calcined). Such vagueness as to what is intended misleads the public and may void the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claims permissible if inventor discloses what he actually uses
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee states the substances which he makes use of himself, and there are still other substances which will produce the effect, and he claims them by a generic description, his claim will not be void for ambiguity, or too broad for his invention, provided the combination is new in respect to all the substances thus referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to claim substitutes generically (e.g., 'chalk or other absorbent earths') so long as the inventor discloses the substances he actually uses and the combinations claimed are equally new. The patent acts permit claiming multiple modes/ingredients if they are part of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give a liberal construction to protect real inventors where whole specification shows claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If, taking the whole together, the court can perceive the exact nature and extent of the claim made by the inventor, it is bound to adopt that interpretation, and to give it full effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts favor construction 'ut res magis valeat quam pereat' (so that a thing may rather have effect than be destroyed). Minor ambiguities should not defeat a patent if the specification as a whole enables understanding of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable a skilled mechanic to make the invention (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The directions for making the thing must be sufficiently certain and specific to enable a skillful mechanic to accomplish the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish (a) whether the specification discloses what the invention is (question for the court on construction) from (b) whether it sufficiently describes the mode of carrying the invention into practice (question for the jury). A 'liberal common sense' construction applies when assessing practical enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the best mode known and circumstances conducive to advantageous operation
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to disclose the most advantageous mode known to him; and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose the best mode or to reveal advantageous operating circumstances can vitiate a patent. Conversely, inserting useless or unnecessary matters purporting to be essential may be presumed intended to mislead and can void the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include more parts than necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If more parts be inserted than are necessary, as ten, where four are sufficient, the specification is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overloading the specification with extraneous parts may render it defective because it fails to give a clear account of what is essential to the invention. Courts have held such excesses can 'blow up' a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show later improvements were made after issuance (best mode / disclosure timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An improved mode of working his machine by the patentee, different from the specification of his patent, casts upon him the burden of showing that he made the improvement subsequently to the issuing of his patent, otherwise it will be presumed that he did not disclose in his specification the best method known to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee uses a better method than described, he must prove the improvement post-dates the patent; otherwise courts may treat the specification as having withheld the best mode and may deny protection or find no infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: If specification does not fully describe everything essential, no infringement by later perfected practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent does not fully describe everything essential to the making or doing of the thing patented, there will be no infringement by the fresh invention of processes which the patentee has withheld from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An infringement is a copy made after and agreeing with the principle laid down in the patent; if essential practical details are omitted, someone who completes or perfects the invention may not infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity from misuse of terms is fatal; trivial word mistakes may be excused if explained elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity produced by a misuse of terms, so as to render the specification unintelligible, will be as fatal as any other defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using 'fossil-salt' when only 'sal-gem' works, or 'chemical white-lead' when no such trade substance exists — these misuses mislead and create unnecessary experiments. However, a mere mistake of one word (e.g., 'painting' for 'printing') can be immaterial if other parts of the patent explain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming an improvement, confine claim to the improvement (not the whole preexisting machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of an improvement, when an improvement is the real subject-matter of the patent, should be made in such a manner as will clearly show that the improvement only is claimed by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a machine substantially existed before, the patentee should not claim the whole machine in its improved state but should be confined to his improvement, even where the improvement is an addition producing the same effects better or new combinations producing new effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite prior use when claiming an improvement to avoid claiming an entire original discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention be an improvement, and be claimed as such, but nothing is said of any previous use, of which the use proposed is averred to be an improvement, the patent may incur the risk of being construed as a claim of entire and original discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid being read as claiming an entire discovery, the specification should recite what had formerly been done and describe how the claimed mode differs and constitutes the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When describing improvement in a known machine, describe parts and effects (not entire machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing the improvement of a machine in use and well known, it is not necessary to state in detail the structure of the entire and improved machine. It is only necessary to describe the improvement by showing the parts of which it consists, and the effects which it produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirements still require clarity: for machines, the patentee 'shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the principle of a machine and all modes of its application that are claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: By the principle of a machine is to be understood the peculiar structure and mode of operation... By explaining 'the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle,' the statute is presumed to direct the patentee to point out all the modes of applying the principle which he claims to be his own invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State not only the peculiar device or construction you prefer, but also all other modes of producing the same effect which you intend to have covered by the patent — whether they are the best modes or mere formal variations.
